title: 1 Kings 3:6–15
context: Solomon answers the LORD’s invitation with a prayer that begins by recalling God’s loving kindness to David, confesses his own inexperience, and asks for an understanding heart to judge God’s people. God is pleased and grants not only wisdom but riches and honor, adding a conditional promise of long life if Solomon walks in God’s ways as David did. Solomon wakes, returns to Jerusalem, and worships before the ark. Both traditions treat the gift of wisdom as largely shared ground: wisdom is God’s gift, Solomon’s humble request is commended, and the conditional promise in verse 14 sits alongside God’s steadfast commitment to David’s house without forcing a sharp divide.

verses.text: Solomon said, “You have shown to your servant David my father great loving kindness, because he walked before you in truth, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart with you. You have kept for him this great loving kindness, that you have given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is today.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon grounds his prayer in God’s great loving kindness to David, while also observing that David walked before God in truth, righteousness, and uprightness of heart. Many Arminian interpreters see here a relationship in which God’s faithfulness and human faithfulness are both real and both named, without making David’s conduct the cause of God’s grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that Solomon himself calls God’s favor to David “great loving kindness” and sees the gift of a son on the throne as God keeping his covenant word (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Both traditions agree that David’s walk is mentioned as the fitting response to grace, and that Solomon’s own kingship is received as a gift rather than claimed as an achievement.

verses.text: Now, LORD my God, you have made your servant king instead of David my father. I am just a little child. I don’t know how to go out or come in.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers are struck by Solomon’s honest confession that he is “just a little child” who does not know how to go out or come in. The phrase likely describes inexperience in leadership rather than literal age, and it models the kind of humility before God that opens a person to receive wisdom rather than relying on self-confidence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see Solomon acknowledging his dependence, noting that he credits God with making him king. Both traditions agree that this self-assessment is the heart of the prayer’s humility: Solomon recognizes that the responsibility God has placed on him exceeds his natural capacity, and that he needs help from the God who appointed him.

verses.text: Your servant is among your people which you have chosen, a great people, that can’t be numbered or counted for multitude.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon describes Israel as the people God has chosen, a great people beyond counting, and many see an echo of the promises to Abraham (Genesis 13:16; 22:17). In this setting, election refers to God’s choice of a nation for his purposes in history, and the king serves among that people rather than above them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s choice of Israel as the foundation of Solomon’s office, and they read the great multitude as evidence that God has kept his promises to the patriarchs. Both traditions agree that the verse concerns God’s corporate choice of Israel as his covenant people, and that the king’s task is to serve that people faithfully as God’s servant.

verses.text: Give your servant therefore an understanding heart to judge your people, that I may discern between good and evil; for who is able to judge this great people of yours?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Solomon asks for an understanding heart to judge God’s people and to discern between good and evil. The request is directed outward toward justice for others rather than personal gain, and Arminian interpreters see in it a sincere moral choice that God honors, showing that the desires a person brings to God matter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Solomon asks God to supply what only God can give, and they see the request itself as evidence of God already at work in his heart. Both traditions agree that the prayer rightly recognizes the people as belonging to God, “this great people of yours,” and that true judgment requires a wisdom received from God rather than mere cleverness.

verses.text: This request pleased the Lord, that Solomon had asked this thing.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon’s request pleased the Lord, and see a real relationship in which God responds with delight to the choices and priorities of his servant. The verse shows that God is not indifferent to what people ask for, and that a request shaped by concern for justice is pleasing to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also emphasize God’s pleasure in Solomon’s request, while seeing that the request itself reflects the work of God, who gives his servants right desires. Both traditions agree that the verse portrays God as personally engaged, and that Solomon’s request is commended because it seeks what serves God’s people rather than what would merely enrich the king.

verses.text: God said to him, “Because you have asked this thing, and have not asked for yourself long life, nor have you asked for riches for yourself, nor have you asked for the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern justice,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that God lists what Solomon did not ask for: long life, riches, or the life of his enemies. The contrast reveals the character of Solomon’s request, and Arminian interpreters stress that God responds to the genuine orientation of a heart that seeks understanding to discern justice rather than its own advantage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same contrast and see in it a pattern found elsewhere in Scripture, where seeking God’s purposes first is accompanied by other blessings (compare Matthew 6:33). Both traditions agree that the verse commends the priority of justice over self-interest, and that God himself is the one who evaluates and honors a request made in that spirit.

verses.text: behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a wise and understanding heart, so that there has been no one like you before you, and after you none will arise like you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers emphasize that God grants Solomon’s request fully, giving him a wise and understanding heart unlike anyone before or after him. The gift is real and lasting, yet Arminian interpreters note that the later story shows that even extraordinary wisdom does not remove the need for continued faithfulness, as Solomon’s later failures make clear (1 Kings 11:1–11).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that wisdom is God’s sovereign gift, given in abundance and beyond Solomon’s merit. Both traditions agree that the verse presents Solomon’s wisdom as unique and as coming entirely from God, and both recognize that the narrative will later show a wise king making unwise choices, a sobering reminder that gifts are not the same as steadfast obedience.

verses.text: I have also given you that which you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that there will not be any among the kings like you for all your days.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that God adds riches and honor, gifts Solomon had not asked for, and see God’s generosity going beyond what was requested. These additional blessings also bring added responsibility, and the later story shows how wealth and honor became part of the temptations Solomon faced, which Arminian interpreters read as a warning about stewardship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in this verse the overflowing generosity of God, who gives more than his servants ask or think. Both traditions agree that riches and honor here are gifts of grace rather than rewards earned, and both note that the narrative will later test how Solomon handles these gifts, showing that blessing must be received with continuing humility.

verses.text: If you will walk in my ways, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers stress the conditional form of this promise: if Solomon walks in God’s ways and keeps his statutes as David did, God will lengthen his days. Many Arminian interpreters see here a genuine condition that leaves Solomon responsible for his response, consistent with the way blessings in Deuteronomy are tied to obedience (Deuteronomy 6:1–3).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also take the condition seriously and see it as part of the covenant structure in which God calls his people to obedience. They hold this alongside God’s unconditional commitment to David’s line (2 Samuel 7:14–16). Both traditions agree that the conditional promise of long life concerns Solomon’s personal blessing, while God’s faithfulness to David’s house remains secure.

verses.text: Solomon awoke; and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the LORD’s covenant, and offered up burnt offerings, offered peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon’s first response upon waking is worship: he goes to Jerusalem, stands before the ark of the covenant, and offers burnt and peace offerings. His response shows gratitude expressed in action, and many see significance in his turning toward the ark as the focus of covenant worship after the dream at Gibeon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see Solomon’s return to the ark as a fitting response to grace, centering his worship on the place associated with God’s covenant presence. Both traditions agree that the feast for his servants extends the joy of God’s gift to others, and that the scene ends with worship as the right response to God’s kindness.
